extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and evaluation of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131(a) and 1.132 (evidence traversing rejections), including timeliness, sufficiency, required allegations, exhibits, and how objective indicia of nonobviousness and nexus are to be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of conception, reasonable diligence, and reduction to practice under 37 CFR 1.131(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms “conception,” “reasonable diligence,” and “reduction to practice” have the same meanings under 37 CFR 1.131(a) as they have in interference proceedings, but Rule 131 practice is for the purpose of antedating a reference and is not necessarily controlled by interference law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Eickmeyer explains the purpose of a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit is to antedate the effective date of a reference rather than to demonstrate prior invention per se; the parallels to interference practice are for convenience rather than necessity; see also In re Borkowski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences from interference practice: utility and corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: One difference is that in interference practice a reduction to practice requires proof that a utility was known, whereas under 37 CFR 1.131(a) proof of a utility must be shown only if the reference discloses a utility. In interference practice conception, reasonable diligence, and reduction to practice require corroboration, whereas averments made in a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration do not require corroboration; an applicant may stand on their own affidavit or declaration if they so elect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether test results are required to establish utility depends on the facts; ultimate issue is whether one of ordinary skill would be satisfied to a reasonable certainty that the subject matter possessed the alleged utility (In re Blake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence requirement and critical period
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence need not be considered unless conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference is clearly established. Diligence comes into question only after prior conception is established. Diligence is binary (an inventor is either diligent at a given time or is not), and inactivity must be excused with explanation in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical period in which diligence must be shown begins just before the effective date of the reference or activity as prior art and ends with the date of reduction to practice, actual or constructive (filing a U.S. patent application). Only diligence before reduction to practice is material. See In re Nelson, In re Steed, and MPEP § 2138.06 for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for insufficient evidence or lack of diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use form paragraphs where evidence is insufficient or diligence is lacking in a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.59.fti or 7.63.fti may be used where insufficient evidence is included in a 1.131(a) affidavit. Form paragraph 7.62.fti may be used to respond where diligence is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference testimony sometimes usable to antedate reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in an interference may sometimes be used to antedate a reference in lieu of a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The part of the testimony forming the basis of priority over the reference should be pointed out (Ex parte Bowyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical requirement for acts relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts relied upon to establish a date prior to the reference must have been carried out in the United States or in a NAFTA or WTO member country; the 1.131(a) affidavit or declaration must contain an allegation to that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 104 restricts establishing a date of invention by activity in foreign countries other than NAFTA or WTO members except as provided. Effective dates: NAFTA on/after Dec 8, 1993; WTO (other than NAFTA members) on/after Jan 1, 1996. Acts before those dates may be relied upon only as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) must comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits that do not comply with 37 CFR 1.91 will be disposed of or returned to applicant at the Office's discretion (see MPEP § 608.03(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision authority and review for 1.131(a) affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of sufficiency of affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131(a) should be reviewed and decided by a primary examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review of formal sufficiency/propriety is by petition under 37 CFR 1.181 (answered by Technology Center Directors); review of merits is by appeal to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely presentation rules for 1.131(a) affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131(a) must be timely presented to be admitted. Affidavits/declarations and other evidence traversing rejections are considered timely if submitted: (A) prior to a final rejection; (B) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (C) after final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why necessary and not earlier presented; or (D) after prosecution is closed if filed with an RCE (37 CFR 1.114) or CPA (37 CFR 1.53(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All admitted affidavits/declarations are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next succeeding action. For affidavits filed after appeal see 37 CFR 41.33(d) and MPEP §§ 1206 and 1211.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review for prior public use/on sale and best mode issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must determine whether affidavits/declarations and accompanying evidence show that the claimed invention was "in public use" or "on sale" more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)). If the 1.131(a) evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode requirement must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A best mode rejection should not be made unless the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (see MPEP §§ 2133.03 and 2165–2165.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations to traverse rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim of an application is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132. It is the primary examiner's responsibility to review and decide whether such affidavits/declarations and other traversing evidence are responsive and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications may be evidence of the facts at issue and should be considered to the extent probative and properly submitted. This rule is the general Office policy for receiving affidavit evidence traversing rejections when not covered by other specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit is a written statement made under oath before an authorized officer; a declaration (per 37 CFR 1.68) may be used instead but must include an acknowledgment that willful false statements are punishable (18 U.S.C. 1001) and that statements of own knowledge are true and statements on information and belief are believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 602 et seq. for additional formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for 1.132 responses and categories of insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 7.65 (affidavit/declaration effective to withdraw rejection) or 7.66 (insufficient) and form paragraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 to explain specific reasons an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for insufficiency categories include: untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane to the rejection; showing not commensurate in scope with claims. Examiner must include detailed explanation of why the affidavit/declaration is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason 7.66.01 — Affiant has never seen the invention before
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit that includes statements amounting to an affirmation that the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before is not relevant to the issue of nonobviousness and provides no objective evidence thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and a full explanation provided if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason 7.66.02 — Affidavit states invention works as intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit statements that the claimed subject matter functions as intended are not relevant to the issue of nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and a full explanation provided if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason 7.66.03 — Refers only to invention, not to individual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit that refers only to the system described in an application and not to the individual claims does not show the objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the affidavit ties evidence to the individual claim limitations; this form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and accompanied by a full explanation if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason 7.66.05 — Conclusion that rebuttal evidence fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When all evidence is considered, the totality of the rebuttal evidence of nonobviousness may fail to outweigh the evidence of obviousness; use form paragraph 7.66.05 to present that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph should conclude the explanation of why the affidavit/declaration is insufficient and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally applicable criteria for traversing evidence: timeliness and consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general criteria applicable to all evidence traversing rejections: (A) timeliness — evidence must be timely/seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration; (B) consideration — timely presented evidence must be considered by the examiner and commented upon in the next action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness specifics are: prior to final rejection; before appeal in non-final cases; after final but before/on date of appeal with showing of good reasons; after prosecution closed only with RCE/CPA. If evidence overcomes the prima facie case, comments should align with reasons for allowance; if insufficient, examiner must specifically explain why (generic statements like "lacks technical validity" are insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) must be considered when timely presented
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention must be considered. While lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of nonobviousness, where a prima facie case of obviousness is established, failure to provide rebuttal evidence is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be probative, secondary consideration evidence must be related (nexus required) to the claimed invention; the applicant/patent owner bears the burden of establishing nexus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nexus is presumed when the evidence is tied to a product that includes the claimed features and is coextensive with them. Presumption fails where product includes critical unclaimed features. Even without presumption, patent owner may prove nexus by showing the objective evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention. Evidence tied to elements in the prior art does not establish nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments presented by the applicant cannot take the place of evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements that are not evidence (and must be supported by affidavit/declaration) include assertions of unexpected results, commercial success, solution of long-felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before the date of the reference, and allegations of derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of opinion evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion testimony is entitled to consideration and some weight so long as the opinion is not on the ultimate legal conclusion at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While an opinion on the ultimate legal issue is not entitled to weight, the underlying basis for the opinion may be persuasive. Expert testimony that is persuasively supported on what was not obvious to the expert may be given some weight; legal conclusions by experts are not evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of commercial success and long-felt need evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence such as commercial success or proof of long-felt need must be factually supported by appropriate affidavit/declaration to be of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law emphasize that unexpected results and commercial success must be established by factual evidence rather than mere assertion (see In re De Blauwe and related cases).
